newsitem.title: USA: U.S. factory orders up, jobless claims down.
newsitem.headline: U.S. factory orders up, jobless claims down.

text.p: Factories hummed with new business in January after an end-of-year slump and jobless claims fell again last week, reports said Thursday, pointing to manufacturing strength and more good-paying jobs ahead.

The reports came after Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan warned repeatedly in recent days that the central bank stood ready to raise interest rates, if necessary, in a bid to ward off inflation.

The Commerce Department said factory orders rose 2.5 percent in January to a seasonally adjusted $323.2 billion -- the best performance in four months -- after falling 1.5 percent in December and 0.5 percent in November.
Shipments of finished products and backlogs of unfilled orders also both rose, signs that industrial activity will stay strong in coming months.

"The industrial sector is on a very sustainable trajectory," economist Bruce Steinberg at Merrill Lynch and Co. said, noting he did not see pressures developing that might push prices and wages up too quickly.
He said some of January's gain was a rebound from weakness as 1996 ended.

The Labour Department said in a separate report that new jobless claims fell 6,000 last week to 310,000. The four-week moving average, seen as a better gauge of jobless trends since it smooths out weekly fluctuations, fell to its lowest level in nearly eight years, also at 310,000.

Marilyn Schaja, an economist with Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp. in New York, noted it was the eighth week in a row that the moving average fell and "clearly indicate(s) a tight labour market."
The increase in January factory orders was the strongest since a 2.6 percent rise last September and covered nearly every type of manufactured product.
Orders for costly durable goods such as new cars and refrigerators rose by 4 percent after falling 1.7 percent in December.
Orders for nondurables like food and paper products grew 0.7 percent after a 1.2 percent December decline.
Orders for transportation equipment -- the single biggest category -- climbed 2.5 percent. Electrical and electronic machinery orders jumped 16.6 percent.
Jerry Jasinowski, president of the National Association of Manufacturers, said booming demand for electronic equipment showed businesses were still aggressively boosting production capacity.
"Capital spending is alive and well," he said. "Fixed investment by business, especially in computers, has been one of the strongest sectors in the 1990s, and this is likely to continue in 1997."
In testimony to Congress on Tuesday, Greenspan said it was "crucial" to keep inflation down and made clear the central bank was ready to raise rates if needed to achieve that.

Some economists believe Greenspan was trying to prepare financial markets for a rate rise should the Fed boost rates in coming months. The Fed's aim would be to keep the economy growing at a moderate pace that would not spur a pickup in inflation. The economy has just entered its seventh year of growth after the last recession ended in March 1991.

There have been other recent signs that a pickup in manufacturing activity continued past January. The National Association of Manufacturers said on Monday that its index of activity rose in February as production and new orders increased.

The Commerce Department said shipments of manufactured goods rose 1.1 percent in January after falling 0.7 percent in December and order backlogs rose for the fifth straight month, pointing to continued manufacturing strength ahead.
